Russia’s oil processing rates have plunged to the lowest in more than two decades as Ukraine continues to strike refineries, according to Rystad Energy, heaping pressure on the country’s domestic fuel supplies.

Ukraine has attacked at least 18 refineries since late October, according to a Bloomberg tally based on statements from officials in both nations and people familiar with the incidents.  (Bloomberg)

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
The Fed’s hawks are reading the wrong chart

Comparing real policy rates across eras means nothing until you adjust for neutral. Do that, and the case for hiking disappears.

The chart is everywhere. In 1995, the real federal funds rate was 3.75%. Today it is zero. So Greenspan leaned against the dotcom boom while the Fed now fuels one, and must hike.

It is wrong three times over.

Neutral has collapsed

The New York Fed’s Holston-Laubach-Williams model put neutral near 3% in the mid-1990s. Today it is just under 1%. A 3.75% real rate was only about three-quarters of a point restrictive. Raw comparisons ignore two points of drift.

The zero is temporary

The zero subtracts an energy-inflated 3.8% PCE reading from a 3.75–4.00% funds rate. Oil is falling. When the base effects roll off in April, PCE returns to 2%, and the real rate rises about 1.75 points with no Fed action.

Add the December hike that futures price at about 96%, and the real rate is 2.1%. That is 1.2 points above neutral, tighter than Greenspan in 1995. A 50 basis point move makes the gap 1.5 points.

Productivity is the real parallel

Greenspan held in 1995 because he bet on faster productivity. Growth ran 1.5% in 1990–95 and 2.5% in 1995–2000. In Q3 productivity rose at a 3.6% annualised rate while unit labour costs fell 0.7%. With GDP above 4%, that is likely revised to 4.8%, lifting the annual pace toward 2.4%. Greenspan had a hunch. The Fed has data.

And Wall St still questions the AI productivity cycle.

Debt raises the stakes

The deficit is 6.2% of GDP, not 2.2%. Hikes lift Treasury refinancing costs and widen the deficit hawks call stimulative. Firms and households carry more short-dated debt than in 1995, so every point bites harder.

Amazing how Wall St assumes an economy with WWII debt levels can sustain rate hikes. 

The verdict

The investment boom is real: information-processing equipment spending grew at a 60% annualised rate in Q3. But it is building capacity. Tightening against it chokes the supply that holds inflation down.

The Fed should hold, as Greenspan did. Policy is already restrictive.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
The Labor Market Is Exhibiting Recessionary Weakness Before Widespread Layoffs

Historically low unemployment claims continue to reinforce the narrative of a resilient labor market. However, employment retention should not be confused with labor market strength. Beneath the surface, several indicators suggest the economy is becoming increasingly vulnerable to a cyclical downturn.

Employment Growth At Historically Concerning Levels

The underlying labor market data reveal a considerably weaker environment than unemployment claims suggest.

•  The hiring rate stands at 3.4% compared with 3.9% in September 2019.

•  Monthly payroll gains averaged just 48,000 over the 12 months preceding October.

•  Involuntary part time employment increased by 339,000 in October.

•  Approximately 27.6% of unemployed Americans have been jobless for at least 27 weeks.

Excluding the pandemic and the current slowdown, the last time rolling annual payroll growth was this weak was October 2010, during the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis. Similar weakness occurred during the jobless recovery following the 2001 recession.

What makes today particularly concerning is that employment growth associated with previous recessionary aftermaths is occurring during an apparent late cycle expansion, before widespread layoffs have even materialized.

The Vulnerability Of A Low Hire Low Fire Economy

Even Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has acknowledged the unusual nature of the current labor market equilibrium.

Businesses can respond to deteriorating economic conditions by freezing hiring, reducing working hours, eliminating overtime and leaving departing employees unreplaced before resorting to layoffs.

Artificial intelligence introduces another structural vulnerability. Companies do not necessarily need to eliminate existing jobs to reduce labor demand. They can suppress future hiring and replacement positions without generating additional unemployment claims.

Consequently, unemployment claims alone cannot capture the full extent of labor market deterioration.

Employment stability increasingly depends on businesses retaining existing workers rather than generating new employment opportunities.

The Late Cycle Implications

The economic environment supporting employment retention is becoming increasingly fragile.

•  Real consumption has grown less than 0.1% over 2 months.

•  Real aggregate wage income is growing just 0.27% annually.

•  Corporate profitability stands at a record 12.2% of GDP.

•  AI financing conditions are deteriorating.

• Persistent inflation is increasing the likelihood of further monetary tightening.

Historically, businesses have responded to weakening demand and profit compression by reducing capital expenditure and labor costs.

With hiring already depressed, even a normalization in layoffs could produce a disproportionately large increase in unemployment. Displaced workers would face fewer employment opportunities, potentially extending unemployment duration and accelerating household financial deterioration.

Declining labor income would further weaken consumption, compress corporate profitability and encourage additional layoffs, creating a self reinforcing economic contraction.

Slower labor force growth partially explains weaker payroll creation, but it does not eliminate the cyclical risks associated with depressed hiring.

Historically, employment growth this weak has reflected an economy absorbing the consequences of a downturn. Today, it may be revealing how little capacity the labor market has to absorb the next one.

posts.name: Dividendology
posts.text:
Your first $100,000 could take 10 years to build.

Going from $900,000 to $1 million? About 1 year.

Same monthly investment. Same assumed return. Same $100,000 increase.

The difference is how much money you already have working for you.

Assuming you invest $500 per month and earn a 10% annual return, compounded monthly, here’s approximately how long each milestone takes:

• $0 → $100K: 10 years
• $100K → $200K: 5 years
• $200K → $300K: 3.4 years
• $300K → $400K: 2.6 years
• $400K → $500K: 2.1 years
• $500K → $600K: 1.7 years
• $600K → $700K: 1.5 years
• $700K → $800K: 1.3 years
• $800K → $900K: 1.2 years
• $900K → $1 million: 1 year

Early on, your contributions drive most of your progress.

A $10,000 portfolio earning 10% generates $1,000 in annual gains. 

Your $6,000 in yearly contributions does most of the heavy lifting.

But a $900,000 portfolio earning 10% generates $90,000 in annual gains, before adding another dollar.

That’s why the beginning feels so slow. 

You’re building the foundation that makes those larger dollar gains possible.

Every contribution adds to that foundation. 

Every reinvested dividend buys more shares. 

And those shares can generate returns of their own.

The first $100,000 requires a lot of patience because you’re doing so much of the work yourself.

Over time, your portfolio can carry more of the load.

That's the snowball effect taking place.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
The Fed Hiked Into a Supply Shock. 

The Bond Market Will Force the Cuts.
The Federal Reserve follows the credit market, and the credit market speaks through the two-year Treasury. In 2007 the two-year peaked more than a year before the first cut. In 2019 it peaked in November 2018 and was 1.89 per cent when the Fed cut in July. In 2024 it peaked in October 2023 and had fallen to 3.61 per cent when the Fed moved in September. The policy rate follows the two-year.

That market is turning. The two-year closed at 4.61 per cent on 25 November, down from a 2026 peak of 4.92 per cent. The 10-year has fallen to 4.85 per cent from 5.31 per cent. The curve slope is only 24 basis points, against a long-run average of 85 to 100. If inflation rolls over, a 4 per cent 10-year and a 3 per cent two-year is the natural configuration.
The Fed has done the opposite. 

The September quarter-point hike was a mistake, because textbook policy looks through energy supply shocks. Now it may hike again in December. Christopher Waller wants a half-point and Alberto Musalem expects several increases.

Then the data will turn. After the December meeting, the month-on-month CPI print will be negative. WTI has already fallen to $82.24 from $114.58, Brent to $91.80 from $138.21, and the 3-2-1 crack spread from $78.92 to about $31. Saudi Arabia lifted October output 26 per cent to 10.56 million barrels a day and cut Asian prices to a six-year low.

The market is ignoring what happens when Saudi Arabia fights for market share. After 2014, WTI fell from $107.95 to $26.19, and weak energy prices lasted for years. The credit market is ignoring the noise and watching the commodity complex. The Fed will be forced to cut, and Wall Street will then proclaim what just happened.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text: The tariff headline that hit the tape on yesterday deserves more than a line, because it is not a tweet, it is a process. The administration is preparing findings from a Section 301 probe into excess industrial capacity across 16 trading partners, with rates up to 20% on China, 15% on the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, and higher still on Vietnam and India. The tariffs could begin in January after hearings, and the US-China truce expires Jan 10, so the calendar is tight. Asia's chip names sold off hard on it, and the US tape followed. The market's fear is not the tariff itself, it is the second-order effect: tariffs on industrial capacity mean higher input costs for the same companies building the AI data centers, and slower global growth while the Fed is hiking. The probe is a process with hearings, which means headlines will keep coming. The trade is not to guess the outcome, it is to know the dates: hearings, January, Jan 10.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text: The bond market disagreed with the inflation print on yesterday , and the bond market is usually the one worth listening to. Core PCE came in a tenth hot, GDP was revised up to a strong number, and the 10-year yield fell anyway, down more than 9 basis points to around 4.81%. Yields fall when the market fears growth more than inflation, and that is the read. The tape sold off on tariff headlines, not on the inflation number, and the bond market said the hiking path is already priced. A December hike is the base case and everyone knows it. What the bond market is pricing now is what comes after: a Fed that hikes into a slowing economy because it has to, not because it wants to. When yields fall on a hot print, the market is telling you the growth scare is the bigger story. Watch the 10-year into Friday. If it keeps falling while stocks bounce, the bond market is calling the recovery a relief rally. If yields stabilize, the growth fear is passing.
